"Threaten" means to signal that something bad, harmful, or dangerous may happen — either because a person deliberately intends to cause it, or because a situation is naturally moving toward it. Whenever this word appears, something harmful is either being promised, looming in the background, or drawing dangerously close.

Sense 1 — A Person Warns Another Person of Harm

This is the sense most people know first. When one person threatens another, they communicate — through spoken words, a written message, or even a physical gesture — that they will do something harmful. The purpose is usually to scare the other person, pressure them into doing something, or show power over them.

The critical ingredient here is intent. A real person is deliberately choosing to make someone else feel fear or pressure.

For example: "He threatened to report her to the police unless she returned the money." Here, he is using the possibility of harm as a weapon to get what he wants. Or: "The gang members threatened witnesses before the trial began." Here, the purpose is pure intimidation — to silence people through fear.

You will often see this structure: threaten + to + verb. "She threatened to quit." "He threatened to expose the truth." "They threatened to sue the company." In each case, a person is saying, in effect, "Do what I want — or else this bad thing will happen."

You will also commonly see: threaten someone with something. "He threatened her with violence." "The manager threatened the employees with termination." Here, the harmful thing is stated as a noun rather than an action.

And sometimes it appears as: threaten that + a full sentence. "He threatened that he would destroy her reputation." This works exactly the same way, just with a fuller description of the intended harm.

One important thing to note: the threat does not have to be carried out for the word to apply. The moment someone signals harmful intent, the act of threatening has occurred. Whether they follow through is a separate matter.

Sense 2 — Something (Not a Person) Poses Danger to Something Else

This is a broader and very important use of the word. Here, the subject doing the "threatening" is not a person with a plan — it is a force, situation, or phenomenon that puts something at risk.

For example: "Rising sea levels threaten coastal cities." The sea has no intention. It is not angry, and it is not trying to pressure anyone. But it still threatens — meaning it puts those cities in danger of being harmed or destroyed.

More examples in the same pattern: "The drought threatens the nation's food supply." "Deforestation threatens the survival of many species." "The virus threatened millions of lives."

Notice the structure here: something threatens something else. The first "something" is the source of danger (drought, deforestation, a disease). The second "something" is what is at risk (food supply, species, lives). There is no human intent involved — just the natural force of one thing endangering another.

This sense is extremely common in news writing, science, and formal discussion.

Sense 3 — Something Bad Seems About to Happen

In this third sense, "threaten" describes a situation that looks like it is heading toward a bad outcome. Think of it as the verb form of "on the verge of something unwanted."

For example: "The argument threatened to turn violent." This means the argument was moving in a direction where violence seemed likely — it hadn't happened yet, but the signs were there. Or: "What began as a small disagreement threatened to become a full-blown crisis." Or: "The project threatened to go over budget."

The structure here is almost always: something threatens to + verb. The thing doing the threatening is a situation, and what it "threatens to do" is the bad outcome approaching.

This sense is closely related to Sense 2, but the subtle difference is that Sense 2 says something is already a source of danger ("droughts threaten crops"), while Sense 3 emphasizes that something bad is about to unfold ("the situation threatened to collapse").

This is worth knowing on its own because it works differently. When you say someone feels threatened, you are describing their emotional state — a feeling of fear, insecurity, or sensing that their safety, status, or wellbeing is in danger. Crucially, nobody necessarily needs to have said anything threatening for this to apply.

For example: "She felt threatened by his aggressive tone." He may not have said "I will hurt you" — but his manner made her feel unsafe. Or: "Some managers feel threatened by employees who are smarter than them." Here, no actual physical danger exists — it is a feeling of one's position or importance being at risk.

This expression captures a psychological experience of threat, not just a literal one.

Threats can be explicit or implied. An explicit threat is stated clearly: "I will hurt you if you don't cooperate." An implied threat uses actions, tone, or situation to communicate the same danger without saying it directly — for example, someone slowly sharpening a knife while staring at you, or a gang standing outside someone's house. "Threaten" covers both.

The word always carries a negative weight. You will never use "threaten" to describe something good that is approaching. It is always tied to harm, danger, loss, or an unwanted outcome.

The subject can be a person, an object, a situation, or a natural force. A criminal can threaten you. A storm can threaten a town. A conflict can threaten peace. The word is flexible in its subject, but what remains constant is the idea of imminent harm or danger.

"Threaten" is often used in the passive voice. "She was threatened at gunpoint." "Endangered animals are threatened by habitat destruction." "He felt he was being threatened." In passive constructions, the focus shifts to the person or thing being endangered, rather than the source of the threat.

Think of "threaten" as a word that lives at the intersection of danger and anticipation. Something harmful has not necessarily happened yet — but it is being promised, it is looming, or it is building up momentum. Whether a person is using words to intimidate another, a disease is putting a population at risk, or a negotiation is on the verge of breaking down completely — in all of these cases, "threaten" is the right word, because in each one, something bad is either being signaled or is drawing close.

If you can hold onto one simple idea, let it be this: to threaten is to bring harm — real or possible, intended or natural — dangerously close to someone or something.
